newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire soldiers desert Kikwit under rebel threat.
newsitem.headline: Zaire soldiers desert Kikwit under rebel threat.

text.p: Government forces on Monday deserted the provincial town of Kikwit on the road to the Zairean capital leaving it open to advancing rebels, residents and senior dignitaries from the region said.
"By five o'clock this afternoon (1600 GMT) the town was open to the rebels. The Zairean army has left," one politician from the region in touch with residents by radio told Reuters.
"Some laid down their weapons, others piled on vehicles with all their equipment and left in the direction of Kinshasa," he said in Kinshasa.
Residents and business sources say rebels earlier captured the town of Idiofa, around 80 km (50 miles) further east, triggering the government army's retreat from Kikwit.
They could not pinpoint how close to Kikwit itself the rebels were on Monday but indicated that the town, 400 km (250 miles) east of Kinshasa, was about to fall.
"Kikwit is on the point of falling. There is no panic and people are calm," one resident said by radio.

Residents said local authorities earlier asked the army contingent there to lay down their weapons and cease any resistance against the rebels who have captured more than half of Zaire's vast territory since last October.
A senior military official in the capital said he was unable to confirm or deny the reports.

Kikwit, which made world headlines because of an Ebola virus epidemic that killed more than 120 people there in 1995, is the commercial capital of Bandundu province supplying most of Kinshasa's domestically produced food.
Analysts have predicted that its fall could have a dramatic psychological effect on the inhabitants of Kinshasa, many of whom originate from the Bandundu region.
Military sources say the senior command has been building up defences at Kenge, 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa, in a bid to halt the rebels before they reach the capital.

Demoralised and poorly paid government troops have rarely put up resistance since the rebel campaign began in the east of the country in October. In many areas they have looted towns before fleeing in the face of the rebel advance.

Residents say concerted efforts by local authorities, church leaders and some soldiers succeeded in preventing serious looting in Kikwit, which has seen waves of soldiers passing through after fleeing earlier fighting further east.
Businessmen fear that the rebels will continue suffocating the capital in a bid to force President Mobutu Sese Seko to surrender power, an uncompromising demand of Kabila.
Despite persistent rumours there is no confirmation yet of an attempt by rebels to enter territory west of Kinshasa to try and cut the capital's supply lines to the Atlantic ocean.
News of fresh rebel gains on Monday coincided with the arrival in Kinshasa of U.S. envoy Bill Richardson.
His visit is seen as an attempt to bolster floundering efforts to bring the chief protagonists in the conflict together for talks before war reaches the sprawling capital.
Richardson was due to meet Mobutu at his Camp Tshatshi residence on Tuesday morning carrying a personal message from President Bill Clinton.
He told reporters on his arrival that he would be flying on to meet Kabila in the rebel-held city of Lubumbashi.
